newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Cariplo, Ambroveneto link in bank shakeup.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Cariplo, Ambroveneto link in bank shakeup.

text.p: Italy's largest savings bank Cariplo has agreed to join forces with Banco Ambrosiano Veneto but the new giant faces a big challenge trying to slim down a large branch network.

The board of the charitable foundation that controls Cariplo -- whose full-name is Cassa di Risparmio delle Provincie Lombarde -- agreed on Monday evening to open full-blown merger talks with Ambroveneto.

A last-minute offer from Banca Commerciale Italiana to link up with Cariplo was spurned by the foundation. This was the latest humiliation for BCI which has been repeatedly left out in the cold as Italy's top banks pair off with eachother.
The move opens the way to creating Italy's largest banking group, measured by number of branches, and its second biggest by assets behind Turin-based rival Istituto Bancario San Paolo di Torino.
The new banking combine, already dubbed AmbroCariplo by the media, will have assets of 252 trillion lire, deposits of 157 trillion lire, around 2,000 branches and just under 35,000 employees.
AmbroCariplo will tower above most of its Italian rivals but it remains a relative midget on the European banking scene where no Italian institution is ranked in the top ten.

Details of the merger plan carried in Italian newspapers said the two banks would retain separate identities for up to six years, suggesting that cost-cutting and rationalisation will be carried out only gradually.

"It appears that the full-scale merger between the two banks will not happen for three to six years. This is very revealing and it would be better if the process were quicker," said an analyst at the Milan office of a European investment bank.

The government has urged Italian banks, regarded as inefficient and overmanned by European standards, to merge with each other and streamline their activities in preparation for the planned launch of a single European currency in 1999.
As the government's tight monetary policies gradually squeeze inflation out of the economy, interest rates have tumbled -- putting pressure on the fat margins that banks have enjoyed for many years.
Italian newspapers reported on Tuesday that the merger would require Ambroveneto to make a substantial capital increase to fund the 6.5 trillion lire ($3.9 billion) merger with Cariplo.
The bank's shares were trading 5.23 percent lower on the Milan bourse at 4,190 lire on Tuesday afternoon as investors recoiled at the prospect of a big cash call.
In a first step, Ambroveneto would pay the Cariplo foundation three trillion lire for a stake of between 30-40 percent of the savings bank.

Ambroveneto would then spin off its banking activities and form a holding company in which the Cariplo foundation would end up holding 29 percent, making it the largest single shareholder in the group.

Other big shareholders in the holding company, which will own the banking activities of both Cariplo and Ambroveneto, would include France's Credit Agricole with round 25 percent. The French bank is currently Ambroveneto's biggest shareholder.
Another 18 percent of the holding company would be held by insurance company Alleanza and a group of Northeast Italian banks. $=1,667
